frameworks.name: Counsel-Based Feedback Model
frameworks.definition: A decision-making discipline that filters feedback from crowd sources and prioritizes input only from named, high-credibility advisors and proven successful peers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi only accepts feedback from high-credibility advisors and specific counselors he respects, rather than from general audience feedback like TikTok comments, because he trusts that counsel from proven successful individuals is more actionable than crowd-sourced input.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Proven successful advisor with track record
claims.mechanism: Proven success creates alignment of incentives and understanding of context; crowd feedback reflects the median perspective rather than earned expertise.
bounded_by: Does not apply when isolation prevents access to quality counsel
Does not apply when the crowd source is domain experts (e.g., customers in the market)

claims.text: High-quality haters exist and are distinguishable from low-quality haters; having high-quality critics indicates something meaningful about the target because criticism from credible sources demands response differently than from unqualified critics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The critic has skin in the game or relevant experience
claims.mechanism: Credibility is signaled by the critic's own accomplishments or relevance to the domain; unqualified critics reflect their own insecurities rather than accurate assessment of the target.
bounded_by: Rare to encounter truly high-quality haters
Most criticism comes from people projecting their own insecurities

claims.text: Once people achieve financial success and credibility, they stop caring as much about criticism from unqualified sources because they are focused on their own goals and outcomes rather than external validation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Individual has achieved some level of success
Individual has developed their own credible projects or business
claims.mechanism: Success and credibility create a reference frame where external criticism from non-peers becomes irrelevant; internal projects become the primary focus of attention.
bounded_by: Early-stage founders without credibility may still be affected by criticism
Insecure high-achievers may continue to monitor unqualified feedback

claims.text: Most people hate because they are projecting their own insecurities, not because they are accurately assessing the target; therefore the quality of hate directed at someone correlates with the target's visibility and success rather than their merit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Insecurity creates a psychological need to diminish others who represent a different reality or higher achievement; higher visibility increases the total volume of insecure projections.
bounded_by: Does not apply to domain-expert critique from qualified peers
Does not account for cases where criticism is based on genuine ethical disagreement

claims.text: Successful people are inherently hateable because they represent outcomes that challenge the worldview of people who have not achieved similar success; therefore receiving hate is not a moral indictment but a predictable consequence of visibility and accomplishment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Success and visibility make someone a target for projection because they represent disconfirming evidence to the worldview of unsuccessful people.

claims.text: Historical religious figures and wisdom traditions across multiple religions experienced gruesome persecution and death; therefore a modern person receiving criticism should expect it as normal rather than viewing it as evidence of wrongdoing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The person has achieved some level of visibility or success
The person is operating with good intent
claims.mechanism: If even universally-agreed-upon positive historical figures faced extreme persecution, then average-quality people should not expect immunity from criticism; it is a feature of visibility, not evidence of merit.
bounded_by: Does not apply to actual wrongdoing or unethical behavior
Does not mean all criticism should be ignored

claims.text: People who feel disconnected from reality or operate from a distorted worldview are difficult to interact with in real life, and cutting ties from such people is a valid boundary rather than a failure of communication.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The person's reality model is significantly different from your own
Communication attempts fail because the frame difference is fundamental
claims.mechanism: When two people perceive events differently at the baseline, communication becomes impossible because the same words map to different referents; agreement on reality is prerequisite for productive interaction.
bounded_by: Does not justify dismissing people with different values or priorities
Does not apply when the reality-model difference is solvable through better information

claims.text: Alex Hormozi follows a book monetization strategy that prioritizes "proof" by demonstrating that the strategies inside the book work by showing them performing well in monetized outputs (e.g., a book about monetization that made 100 million in weekend sales).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Proof via monetized outcome demonstrates both the viability of the strategies and the commercial viability of the information; this is harder to fake than testimonials alone.
bounded_by: Does not work for all types of content (e.g., pure narrative or memoir)

examples.text: When a TikTok comment gets 27,000 likes criticizing Alex Hormozi, he evaluates it by comparing the critic's actual accomplishments (e.g., do they have $1.2 billion in liquid cash) rather than treating the like count as validation; he then discusses the criticism with his high-credibility advisors to get their perspective on whether it points to something real.

Some high-quality haters of Alex Hormozi exist and have chosen to build criticism of him as a business model (e.g., using his hateable status as a content angle); this is distinguished from low-quality haters who are simply projecting insecurity.

Alex Hormozi is objectively hateable by certain demographics due to his visible attributes and success (tall, physically fit, wealthy, married to an attractive spouse, founded a billion-dollar company, has a young daughter); the hateability is not a reflection of wrongdoing but of how the attributes make him a visual target for people with different life circumstances.

practices.text: When receiving criticism or hate, ask yourself: is this person operating from reality or a distorted worldview? If distorted, treat it as a signal that they are not in your counsel group rather than as valid feedback.
Build and maintain a small council of high-credibility advisors whose opinion you explicitly solicit on criticism you receive, rather than responding to crowd feedback.
When attacked, reflect on your willingness to accept criticism from credible sources; if a critic has earned credibility, their perspective deserves consideration regardless of tone.
